analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and insurers to publish their actual negotiated prices for care.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors in January 2025, the bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes into law requirements that hospitals and health insurance plans disclose their real prices: hospitals must post their full list of standard charges, including the rates they negotiate with each insurer, their cash-pay discounts, and billing codes, for at least 300 common schedulable services, in a free, machine-readable format. Insurance plans must publish in-network and out-of-network rates and the net prices they pay for prescription drugs after rebates, and must give patients a searchable tool to estimate what a specific service will cost them out of pocket. Hospitals that do not comply face a civil penalty of up to $300 per day.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, especially people paying cash (the uninsured or those with high deductibles) and anyone scheduling non-emergency care, who could compare real prices across hospitals and providers before committing to treatment. People with insurance could get an estimate of their own out-of-pocket share before a procedure, instead of being surprised by a bill weeks later.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish, in plain language and free of charge, a machine-readable list of standard charges including gross charges, the specific rates negotiated with each insurer, the minimum and maximum negotiated rates, and the discounted cash price, for at least 300 shoppable services.
Hospitals can satisfy the disclosure requirement by maintaining a free online price estimator, searchable by service, billing code, and insurer, that tells a consumer what they will actually owe.

Insurance plans must publish in-network provider rates, out-of-network allowed amounts, and the negotiated rates and historical net prices (after rebates and discounts) for covered prescription drugs, and must apply these rules to group plans, not just individual marketplace plans.

Plans must provide a free internet self-service tool that gives real-time estimates of a member's cost-sharing for a covered item or service at a specific provider, plus a paper response mailed within two business days on request.
Hospitals that fail to disclose and do not complete a corrective action plan face a civil monetary penalty of up to $300 per day of ongoing violation.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers bear the cost of compiling and publishing detailed price data and building consumer-facing tools. Hospitals also risk losing pricing power where publishing negotiated rates reveals they charge some insurers or cash patients far more than others. Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers would have to expose the rebates and discounts they receive on prescription drugs, information that today largely stays confidential.

drawbacks.text: The penalty for a hospital that simply refuses to comply is capped at $300 per day — roughly $110,000 a year — which is small relative to large hospital systems' revenues and is weaker than the existing regulatory penalty structure for some large hospitals, so enforcement could amount to little.

Transparency alone does not force prices down: a patient facing an emergency cannot shop, and research on price transparency is mixed, with some evidence that publishing negotiated rates can lead providers and insurers to match toward the higher disclosed rates rather than compete downward.

Requiring disclosure of at least 300 shoppable services, with payer-specific rates and billing codes, imposes real compliance and data-management costs, which fall hardest on small and rural hospitals with thin administrative staffs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: patients scheduled for surgery, imaging, or other planned care could see what they will owe before treatment, and cash payers could find hospitals' discounted prices. But the bill's design blunts its own impact — the penalty cap is trivial for large hospital systems, and transparency changes behavior only where patients actually have a choice and time to choose. On the cost side, hospitals and insurers already operate under very similar disclosure requirements adopted by regulation in 2019 and 2020, so the added compliance burden is modest; the main new exposure is for insurers and drug middlemen, who would have to reveal rebate economics they now keep confidential. A reasonable person could support this as a consumer right-to-know measure while conceding it will not, by itself, bring hospital prices down.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action on it, so no vote has happened and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Warren Davidson (R-OH) introduced the bill on January 9, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
The committee has held no markup, hearing, or floor action on the bill; the only entries in the action history are introduction and committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and insurers are better off for now: the current pricing system, where negotiated rates and drug rebates stay largely confidential, remains in place because nothing has moved. Patients gain nothing until a bill like this becomes law.

for.name: Rep. Warren Davidson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write hospital and insurer price disclosure requirements into statute.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has not scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote; it has sat untouched since January 2025.

against.name: Rep. Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, controls the committee's agenda and has not brought the bill up for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to split: the bill has a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and has never been considered by the committee or the floor.

industries.note: Hospitals must publish negotiated rates, cash discounts, and billing codes for at least 300 schedulable services, which erodes their ability to charge different payers very different secret prices, though the $300/day penalty cap limits the downside of ignoring it. The compliance burden falls on hospitals, but most already face similar disclosure rules issued by regulation.

Insurers must publish in-network and out-of-network rates and provide free price-estimator tools for members, and the requirement would now cover employer group plans as well as marketplace plans. Their business depends partly on opaque negotiated pricing, so disclosure works against them even as it is sold as a consumer service.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug rebate intermediaries
industries.note: Plans would have to disclose negotiated drug rates and 'historical net prices' after rebates, discounts, and fees, exposing the rebate economics that PBMs and insurers currently keep confidential. This is the part of the bill with the most direct bearing on why patients' drug prices are far higher than what insurers actually pay.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action more than a year into the Congress, the bill is very unlikely to advance on its own. Price transparency measures of this kind more often move when attached to a larger health package; a watcher should look for whether its language reappears in a broader bill rather than expect standalone action.
